edits.value_json: 你 means “you.” Its visible form combines 亻, treated as the person-category element in one proposed analysis, and 尔, the simplified form of 爾; 爾/尔 was also used for “you/your.” The competing formation analyses remain unresolved, and this history does not establish a sound role for 尔 in 你.

One reported analysis is phonosemantic: 亻 supplies the person category and 尔 a sound cue. A competing, unverified proposal reads 人 and 尔 together as “person” and “you.” The formation remains disputed because the available historical accounts do not directly establish how 你 was formed.

In one reported phonosemantic analysis, 亻 represents a person and contributes the semantic category. A competing proposal treats 人 and 尔 together ideographically; the available evidence does not establish 亻’s historical role in 你.

The right-side 尔 is proposed as the phonetic element. It is the standardized simplified form of 爾, which was used for “you/your”; 尔 is also described as a shortened form of 爾. In Modern Mandarin, 尔 ěr and 你 nǐ differ, and this comparison alone does not establish an ancient sound relationship or 尔’s role in 你.

The present-day Mandarin readings ěr and nǐ do not establish an ancient sound relationship or 尔’s phonetic role in 你. One supplied secondary account gives Old Chinese *njelʔ for 尔 and *nɯʔ for 你, but these are not an independently verified matched comparison here.
In Modern Mandarin, 尔 is ěr and 你 is nǐ. This comparison alone does not demonstrate an ancient sound relationship or 尔’s role in 你.
second-person pronoun, “you”
Current use; historical examples are cited in 集韻 and other works, but exact priority and dating remain unresolved

你 is a current second-person pronoun meaning “you.” Dictionaries cite the gloss 汝也 (“you”) and historical second-person examples; these do not establish the exact earliest surviving occurrence or date the wording of the quoted passages.

The evidence reviewed does not establish whether 尔 originally depicted an object or provide an independently recoverable pronunciation for any such object-name. This limits an object-name borrowing account; it does not by itself resolve 尔’s proposed role in 你.
